extracted.intended_audience: members of the Royal Society / natural philosophers and experimental scientists (17th-century readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing detailed experimental and observational reports in natural philosophy: record conditions, methods, measurements, and comparisons so other learned readers can evaluate and reproduce the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record environmental and contextual conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Report ambient and contextual data (weather, wind direction, thermometer reading, barometer reading, moon phase, season, exact location, relation of storage to street etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page gives examples: wind (south-west), thermometer indicating unseasonal heat for March, barometer 29+ inches, moon past last quarter, and the larder’s position relative to street. Such contextual measurements help interpret observed phenomena (e.g., luminescence, freezing events).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess specimen condition by sensory indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge freshness or putrefaction by sensory signs such as smell, texture, and visible conditioning before asserting causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the veal 'judged very fresh and well conditioned, and fit to be dressed' because 'not the least degree of stench was perceivable' — used to argue luminescence is not simply a product of putrefaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple experimental manipulations/controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Test a phenomenon by exposing the specimen to different treatments (e.g., alcohol, water, vacuum) and compare outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: luminous veal pieces placed in spirit of wine (light vanished in ~15 minutes), in cold water (light persisted >1 hour), and in an exhausted receiver with progressive removal of air (gradual diminution). Contrasting treatments reveal properties of the luminous matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe and report time-course and repeat observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Record how phenomena change over time and repeat experiments to confirm consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: luminous piece observed to shine for 3 days, decay by 4th/5th/6th days and disappear by 7th; vacuum experiment repeated 'once more with like success.' Day-by-day tracking and repetition inform durability and variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for confounders and alternative explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly consider and rule in/out alternative causes (e.g., putrefaction, heat, instrument artefacts) when interpreting results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: authors question whether luminescence is due to putrefaction, using lack of stench and time-course to argue it may be independent; bubble experiment distinguishes thermal rarefaction from atmospheric weight changes by consulting the barometer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify measurements and estimate error
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide numerical measurements (parallax in seconds, barometer inches, lengths) and compare with prior values to assess accuracy and error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: astronomical parallax judged 'certainly not 30 seconds' and 'I believe the sun's parallax is not more than 10 seconds.' Also use barometer readings to corroborate bubble behavior; point out Tycho's errors of 'five minutes at least' in star places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare observations with prior literature/authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and compare specimens or results with previously published descriptions or authorities to aid identification and interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the mushroom description is compared with Job. Bauhin's Fungus piperatus albus; Mr. Ray's reply notes agreement and minor differences. Use of prior taxonomic descriptions helps identify species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear, general rules and illustrate with worked examples
rubrics_metrics.description: When proposing a general method or algorithm (e.g., for drawing tangents), state procedural rules clearly and follow with multiple worked examples and special cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sluse gives stepwise rules for transforming an equation to find a tangent, then works through many example equations and special sign/case distinctions, noting how to distinguish edge cases (parallel tangents, infinite a, sign changes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit methods and claims to peer scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly present methods or inventions for the censure/approval of learned peers rather than asserting them uncritically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I send ... my method ... and submit it to the censure of the learned men of the Royal Society.' This invites critique and validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish causal mechanisms via instrumentation and prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use instruments to test causal hypotheses and predict instrumental responses to observational indicators to confirm cause (e.g., barometer response to bubble position).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Boyle predicted barometer mercury position from bubble behavior; consulting the baroscope verified the conjecture, distinguishing atmospheric weight changes from thermal expansion effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose, test, and replicate multiple specimens; select best for study
rubrics_metrics.description: When specimens are difficult to prepare identically, make multiple attempts/specimens, test them, and select the fittest for detailed observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: N.B.: 'it is very difficult to poise several bubbles precisely ... it is not amiss, to poise a greater number of bubbles together, that, after trial made of all, the fittest may be chosen.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Report negative, inconclusive, or partial results and remaining doubts
rubrics_metrics.description: Record unsuccessful attempts, limitations of methods, and points of doubt rather than hiding them; use them to refine interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: inability 'to effect' an ocular demonstration of veins 'to our mind'; freezing experiments 'did not succeed as we promised ourselves'; explicit admission of remaining doubt about how long light would vanish in an exhausted receiver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe experimental apparatus and procedures in sufficient detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Give concrete descriptions of sizes, materials, manipulations and apparatus so others can repeat the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include blowing small round glass-bubbles 'about the size of hazel nuts' with short stems, putting luminous pieces into crystalline phials or china cups, using a pump and exhausted receiver — all specific set-up details that enable reproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use microscopy and dissection to support anatomical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ microscopes and careful dissections (transverse cuts, stripping fibres) to reveal internal structure underlying macroscopic observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: microscope shows many veins contributing to a drop in a leaf; transverse cuts reveal 'bloody orifices' and thin membranous pipes; stripping fibres exposes veins like small hairs or pipes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogy and comparative reasoning cautiously to infer function
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare observed phenomena to better-known analogues (e.g., plant veins to animal veins) to hypothesize function, while supporting the analogy with experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors argue veins in plants are membranous like animal veins and cite shared behaviours (coagulation on exposure) and mechanical properties (stretch/restore) as evidence, but still rely on experiments and admit difficulties tracing the system fully.
